summary: Kole Jain redesigns common apps (YouTube, Amazon, Gmail, a fitness app, Uber, Figma, Instacart, Apple Books, a recipe site and a smart home app) with deliberately passive-aggressive or infuriating features, as a comedy piece. Most of the ideas are anti-patterns: usage-shaming pop-ups with an upsell, locking Gmail to one browser unless you watch an ad, a modal that blocks everything until you name a layer, paywalls or account walls on a simple recipe, and punishments for breaking a reading streak. Even while being annoying, he keeps one good-UX habit in three of them (the Figma naming modal, the Apple Books streak punishment and the smart home pairing): a notice, a button or a setting to turn the feature off. He also points out where a joke idea could turn useful, such as a driver chattiness rating, or a one-click cart if it were based on past orders and showed a cart total. For someone building a design system, the video works mainly as a list of patterns to avoid and a reminder that any forcing feature needs an escape hatch [inferred].
key_ideas: Endless pop-ups, paywalls that block content and pointless premium subscriptions can make websites annoying as hell.
A message that shames users about their usage, then offers only an upsell or more notifications, might help someone controlling screen time but mostly just made the presenter angry.
Guilt-tripping copy can slide from passive-aggressive to simply aggressive; the presenter deliberately held back.
Suggesting that a struggling user lower their goal makes a guilt pop-up even worse.
Being annoying is no excuse to ignore good UX: tell users how to turn an intrusive feature off.
A modal that blocks every other action until a chore is done (naming a layer) is something designers would despise about a minute into using it.

Three of the hostile features come with a way out: the optional Figma naming feature has a notice on how to turn it off, the Apple Books streak punishment has a button to turn it off, and smart home pairing can be turned off in settings.
A random one-click cart is useless; basing it on past orders and showing a cart total could make it useful.
Some joke ideas turn out useful, like rating an Uber driver's chattiness so riders can plan the trip.
Requiring a subscription or an account for something as simple as a recipe would make the presenter mad.
Punishing a broken streak (making readers guess where they were in a book) is presented as a feature users will hate.
Letting other people control your smart home devices needs an off switch in settings, and would be far worse for smart locks.

rules.rule: Do not fill a site with endless pop-ups, paywalls in front of content or premium subscriptions that add nothing.
rules.why: The video opens by naming these as what makes websites annoying.
rules.evidence: endless pop-ups pay walls blocking or content

rules.rule: Give every intrusive feature a visible way to turn it off: a button beside it or a switch in settings.
rules.why: Even the deliberately annoying features keep this piece of good UX; the presenter expects users to hate them.
rules.evidence: Apple Books: an even handier button below that to turn this feature off; Smart Home: we need to be able to turn this off in settings

rules.rule: When a feature blocks the user with a modal, include a notice in it that explains how to turn the feature off.
rules.why: Being annoying does not mean ignoring good UX.
rules.evidence: Figma: I added a notice here to let the user know how to turn it off

rules.rule: Do not use a modal that blocks every other action until the user finishes a chore such as naming a layer.
rules.why: It is presented as infuriating; designers would despise it about a minute into using it.
rules.evidence: this model that won't let you do anything else until you name it

rules.rule: Do not shame users about how much they use the product (videos watched, time spent browsing), especially when the only choices offered are an upsell or continued notifications.
rules.why: The YouTube message could help someone controlling screen time but mostly just made the presenter angry; the Amazon browsing-time pop-up is another of the deliberately infuriating changes.
rules.evidence: you can either subscribe to YouTube premium or keep getting these notifications

rules.rule: Do not write guilt-tripping or passive-aggressive messages about a user's progress, such as telling them they would need to run a marathon today to hit their step goal.
rules.why: The video uses this tone on purpose to make apps infuriating; the presenter held back from adding more because it would go from passive-aggressive to simply aggressive.
rules.evidence: you'd need to run a marathon today to hit your goal

rules.rule: Do not pair a progress warning with a button that suggests the user change their goal.
rules.why: The presenter says this would make the fitness pop-up even worse.
rules.evidence: adding a button to change the goal and suggesting that they do so

rules.rule: Do not lock a web app to one browser or make users watch an ad to get access.
rules.why: It is one of the imagined changes designed to make users mad.
rules.evidence: an option to watch a minute long ad to get access to your Gmail

rules.rule: Do not put a paywall or an account requirement in front of simple content such as a recipe.
rules.why: The presenter says requiring a subscription just to make a meal would make him mad.
rules.evidence: restricted with either a pay wall or requiring you to make an account

rules.rule: Base one-click shortcuts, like an auto-filled cart, on the user's past behaviour rather than randomness, and show a running total.
rules.why: A random cart is entirely useless; one based on past orders might be useful, and a cart total helps people keep on budget.
rules.evidence: Instacart: if this was based on your past orders ... add a cart total to help you keep on budget

rules.rule: Do not punish users for breaking a streak, for example by making them guess where they were in a book.
rules.why: It is presented as a punishment feature the presenter expects users to hate; even so, he adds a button to jump to the actual page and one to turn the feature off.
rules.evidence: when you break your streak as sort of a punishment it makes you guess

rules.rule: Consider showing a crowd-sourced rating of a trait that helps users plan, such as a driver's chattiness rating with the number of reviews it is based on.
rules.why: The presenter says this one could actually be pretty useful: riders can plan the trip and not feel awkward in silent moments.
rules.evidence: Uber: there's this chattin rating based on 134 reviews

decisions.question: Should an intrusive or opinionated feature be forced on everyone, or optional with an easy way to turn it off?

options.name: Forced, always on
options.effect: Users cannot switch it off, or can escape only by paying or watching an ad, as with the YouTube watch-time notifications and the Gmail browser lock; the video presents these as infuriating.
options.when: Never, according to the video's framing [inferred].

options.name: Optional, with a way out
options.effect: The feature is switched on by choice and shows a notice, a button or a setting to turn it off, so even an annoying feature respects good UX.
options.when: When a feature blocks, restricts or nags the user; the video does this for the Figma naming modal, the Apple Books streak punishment and the smart home pairing.

decisions.recommendation: Give it a way out: the presenter adds a turn-off notice, button or setting because being annoying does not mean ignoring good UX.
decisions.evidence: Figma: I added a notice here to let the user know how to turn it off

decisions.question: What should a one-click smart shortcut, like an auto-filled grocery cart, be based on?

options.name: Random picks
options.effect: One click pulls up a random cart of goods; the presenter calls it entirely useless in practice.

options.name: The user's past orders, with a cart total
options.effect: The cart reflects what the user actually buys, and a visible total helps them keep on budget.
options.when: When you want the shortcut to save real time.

decisions.recommendation: Base it on past orders and add a cart total; that version might actually be sort of useful.
decisions.evidence: Instacart: if this was based on your past orders then this might actually be sort of useful

examples.visual_note: A brutally honest message about the excessive time spent on YouTube (342 videos is a lot), and the only choices are to subscribe to YouTube Premium or keep getting these notifications. It shows a guilt message paired with an upsell.
After an exorbitant amount of browsing, a pop-up with a sassy message prompts the user to buy a book instead of spending so much time on Amazon.
Gmail is shown as no longer available on Safari or any browser other than Chrome, with an option to watch a minute-long ad to get access. The same screen is applied to Google Drive.
A phone pop-up says you would need to run a marathon today to hit your goal of 10,000 steps a day for the week; a worse version adds a button suggesting you change the goal.

While Uber looks for drivers, the driver pops up with a chattiness rating below, based on 134 reviews, saying he is a 3 out of five in chattiness, so riders can plan for silent moments. The presenter thinks this could be useful.

examples.what: Forced layer naming with a blocking modal
examples.visual_note: When switched on, new layers get a blank name; clicking anywhere except the name field brings up a modal that blocks everything until the layer is named, with a notice explaining how to turn the feature off.
One click fills a random cart of goods. The presenter says it would only be useful if based on past orders, ideally with a cart total.

examples.what: Pay for the person behind you at checkout
examples.visual_note: A checkout option borrowed from drive-thrus, applied to orders that are usually 20 plus items for over $100.

Apple Books has a streak counter at the bottom; after a broken streak the reader drags a slider to guess where they were in the book, with a button to jump to the actual page and another to turn the feature off.

examples.what: Recipe behind a paywall or account wall
examples.visual_note: A dinner recipe is restricted by a paywall or a make-an-account requirement, mirroring finance sites that charge to read articles.

examples.what: Neighbours pairing to your smart home devices
examples.visual_note: Other people can pair to your outlets and light bulbs and turn them on or off; the feature can be turned off in settings, and the presenter notes it would be far worse for smart locks.

caveats: This is a comedy video: every feature is deliberately bad. The rules here are drawn from what the presenter frames as infuriating, plus the few places he names good UX, not from a stated guideline.
Self-promotion: the description promotes the presenter's Newform design community (11k+ designers), the presenter jokes that Uber should hire him, and he asks viewers to subscribe.
The presenter credits inspiration to a person the captions spell 'saurin', who has written a book on this sort of thing; the name is not verified.
The mockups are only described in narration; no media list exists for this video, so visual details come from the transcript alone.
Yummly appears only in the description timestamps; the spoken transcript just says 'a recipe'.

Auto-caption errors: 'model' means modal, 'street counter' means streak counter, 'chattin rating' means chattiness rating, 'random card of goods' means random cart of goods, 'pass aggressive' means passive-aggressive, and 'Mr s' is an unclear driver name.
Published 2024-07-30; the app behaviours described are imagined, not real features of those products, except the Apple Books reading streak counter, which the presenter describes as already there.
